ask: What is the MOST appropriate next management?
options: Discharge because transient synovitis is the most common cause of limping.
Perform a routine growth chart review before assessing the joint.
Start a month of oral prednisolone because inflammation is high.
Diagnose transient synovitis and give NSAIDs alone without review.
Obtain urgent orthopaedic assessment for aspiration/drainage and empiric IV antibiotics after feasible cultures.
explanations: Common does not mean safe when Kocher-type high-risk features are present.
Growth matters in paediatrics but not before an infected joint emergency.
Steroids without infection control may worsen septic arthritis.
Fever, inability to bear weight and marked inflammation strongly suggest septic arthritis.
Correct: septic hip can destroy cartilage and cause sepsis, requiring prompt source control.
pearl: An irritable hip with fever and inability to weight-bear is septic arthritis until excluded.
pivot: A playful afebrile child after viral illness with normal CRP and full weight-bearing may have transient synovitis.

steps: IV access, assess sepsis and give analgesia; blood cultures.
Urgent hip aspiration and surgical washout under paediatric orthopaedics.
Early empiric IV therapy after rapid cultures where feasible; target organism when identified.
Physiotherapy and follow-up for avascular necrosis/growth issues.
management.safety: Do not delay antimicrobials for aspiration if the child is septic or unstable.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

context: Advanced surgical and acute speciality decisions
stem: A 3-month-old previously thriving infant has sudden bilious vomiting, increasing lethargy and abdominal tenderness. Radiograph is nonspecific. Lactate is elevated and BP beginning to fall.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Treat only as gastroenteritis with oral rehydration.
Begin rapid neonatal/paediatric surgical resuscitation and urgent exploration for possible midgut volvulus.
Schedule outpatient upper GI contrast study in two weeks.
Give oral anti-reflux medication and review after 24 hours.
Feed a small amount of milk to assess whether vomiting recurs.
explanations: Bilious emesis and ischaemic physiology are surgical red flags.
Correct: vascular compromise from volvulus can lead to necrosis; operation should not wait in unstable infant.
A deteriorating infant needs emergency surgery, not delayed investigation.
Reflux is non-bilious and does not cause shock.
Bilious vomiting and shock risk suggest intestinal obstruction/ischaemia.
pearl: Bilious vomiting in infants is malrotation/volvulus until excluded; peritonitis or shock pushes directly toward surgery.
pivot: A stable neonate with bilious vomiting may undergo urgent upper-GI contrast confirmation under surgical supervision.

steps: NPO, NG decompression, IV fluids/glucose, lactate and antibiotic coverage if bowel ischaemia suspected.
Urgent surgeon-led exploration and Ladd procedure/viability assessment.
PICU/neonatal transport and sepsis/short-bowel complication monitoring.
management.safety: Do not rely on a normal plain radiograph to rule out volvulus.
management.local: Study summary only: obtain appropriate consultant and multidisciplinary guidance, verified drugs and local operative protocols.

stem: A 71-year-old has four weeks of progressive painless jaundice, dark urine and pale stools. She has lost 6 kg, has a palpable nontender gallbladder and ultrasound reveals dilated intra-/extrahepatic bile ducts.
ask: Which investigation is MOST appropriate next?
options: Give haematinics and review after bilirubin normalises.
Perform elective colonoscopy as first and only investigation.
Prescribe oral antibiotics alone because jaundice is always cholangitis.
Perform urgent pancreatic-protocol CT with specialist hepatopancreatobiliary referral to define obstruction and stage possible malignancy.
Order repeat fasting lipid profile as definitive diagnosis.
explanations: Cholestatic obstruction warrants timely imaging and tissue-directed pathway.
Colonoscopy does not assess pancreaticobiliary obstruction.
No fever/pain suggests malignant obstruction rather than acute biliary infection.
Correct: painless obstructive jaundice with weight loss raises pancreatic head/biliary malignancy suspicion.
Lipids cannot establish site or cause of duct obstruction.
pearl: Courvoisier sign with painless progressive jaundice suggests malignant distal obstruction rather than gallstones.
pivot: Fever, RUQ pain and hypotension would trigger a cholangitis resuscitation and urgent drainage pathway.

steps: LFTs, coagulation, pancreatic-protocol contrast CT and HPB/MRCP/EUS pathways.
Assess resectability and metastases with multidisciplinary HPB review; obtain tissue when indicated.
Consider ERCP stenting for cholangitis, severe symptoms or surgical/oncological planning.
Nutrition, fat-soluble vitamin issues and patient-centred counselling.
management.safety: Do not delay evaluation for spontaneous jaundice resolution.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

context: Advanced GP psychiatry ethics and safe prescribing
stem: A 73-year-old woman presents to GP with a new persistent unilateral headache, scalp tenderness and jaw pain while chewing. She had temporary blurring of vision yesterday. She is afebrile, BP normal, ESR pending.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate GP response?
options: Treat as tension headache with simple analgesics and review in six weeks.
Refer for urgent same-day evaluation and start glucocorticoid treatment when giant-cell arteritis is suspected.
Order MRI in three months without treatment.
Recommend self-massage of temporal artery to improve blood flow.
Give empiric antibiotics for temporal arteritis.
explanations: Jaw claudication and visual symptoms are highly concerning for GCA.
Correct: threatened visual loss demands treatment before ESR/biopsy confirmation.
Delaying therapy may cause permanent blindness.
Massage does not treat arterial inflammation and delays care.
GCA is immune-mediated vasculitis, not a typical infection.
pearl: GCA causes irreversible visual loss; treat suspected cranial disease immediately and confirm later.
pivot: Migraine typically begins earlier in life and lacks jaw claudication/systemic inflammatory features.

steps: Urgent vision symptom screen, temporal tenderness and PMR signs; ESR/CRP, platelets.
High-dose glucocorticoid according to visual-threatening pathway; discuss IV therapy with eye specialist.
Urgent ophthalmology/rheumatology for ultrasound or biopsy and long-term planning.
Glucose, BP, bone and gastric risk monitoring during treatment.
management.safety: Never wait for normal ESR to exclude GCA if clinical suspicion high.
management.local: Educational teaching, not individual clinical orders. Apply current local mental health law, safeguarding procedures and medication monitoring requirements.

stem: A 70-year-old with COPD exacerbation has received inhaled bronchodilators, corticosteroid and controlled oxygen. ABG on titrated oxygen: pH 7.26, PaCO2 78 mmHg, PaO2 65 mmHg. He is awake, cooperative, protecting airway, with moderate work of breathing.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate next respiratory intervention?
options: Increase oxygen to 100% by non-rebreather irrespective of saturation.
Discharge on oral antibiotics because the PaO2 is above 60 mmHg.
Intubate immediately in every hypercapnic COPD patient irrespective of NIV suitability.
Give repeated sedative doses to suppress respiratory effort without further review.
Commence monitored non-invasive ventilation with targeted oxygen and early reassessment of clinical state and ABG.
explanations: Uncontrolled high oxygen can worsen hypercapnia and does not directly support ventilation.
Acidaemic hypercapnic respiratory failure needs inpatient ventilatory support and monitoring.
Intubation is needed if NIV contraindicated or failing; selected patients benefit from trial of NIV.
Sedatives may precipitate hypoventilation and loss of airway protection.
Correct: persistent hypercapnic respiratory acidosis with suitable consciousness/airway makes NIV an evidence-based intervention.
pearl: NIV is indicated for selected COPD exacerbations with persistent acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis despite initial treatment.
pivot: If drowsy, unable to protect airway, severely unstable or rapidly deteriorating, invasive ventilation may be safer.

steps: Controlled oxygen usually aiming 88–92% unless individually indicated, bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics if criteria met.
Begin monitored bilevel NIV in appropriate unit; check mask fit, comfort, patient synchrony and contraindications.
Repeat ABG and clinical work of breathing within protocol times; monitor aspiration, hypotension and deterioration.
Critical care/intubation if worsening pH, consciousness, secretion burden or NIV intolerance.
management.safety: Titrate oxygen to physiologic need; avoid indiscriminate high-concentration oxygen in CO2 retainers.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A 7-year-old has palpable purpura over legs and buttocks, ankle pain and mild colicky abdominal discomfort. Platelet count is normal. Urinalysis has 1+ blood but no protein; BP and renal function are normal.
ask: Which follow-up approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Give immediate high-dose IV immunosuppression to all affected children.
Start prophylactic anticoagulation because palpable purpura indicates thrombosis.
Request skin biopsy routinely before assessing urine or blood pressure.
Reassure and discharge with no further testing because skin rash is self-limiting.
Provide supportive symptom care with scheduled BP and urine protein/blood checks and renal referral if abnormalities progress.
explanations: Most mild IgA vasculitis is self-limiting; treatment depends on organ severity, not rash alone.
IgA vasculitis is small-vessel inflammation, not an indication for routine anticoagulation.
Classic palpable purpura with normal platelets is a clinical diagnosis; renal surveillance is more important.
Renal involvement may develop after rash onset and warrants serial urinalysis/BP even when initially mild.
Correct: monitor for delayed nephritis, hypertension and significant proteinuria.
pearl: IgA vasculitis is a systemic small-vessel vasculitis; the long-term risk is renal, not the rash.
pivot: If significant proteinuria, impaired eGFR or hypertension develops, prompt nephrology evaluation and kidney-directed treatment are needed.

steps: BP, urine dip/UPCR if indicated, renal function, abdominal exam for intussusception, testicular pain and joint symptoms.
Analgesia and hydration; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment or GI bleeding; treat severe abdominal/joint symptoms under paediatric advice.
Document a scheduled serial BP/urine surveillance plan over subsequent months.
Nephrology for persistent/progressive proteinuria, hypertension or renal dysfunction; ED for GI bleeding/severe pain.
management.safety: Absence of proteinuria on day one does not end renal surveillance.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: A 45-year-old reports a sudden 'worst-ever' thunderclap headache that peaked within seconds 13 hours ago, with vomiting and neck pain. He is alert with normal neurological examination. Non-contrast CT head done now is reported normal.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Arrange emergency LP and/or vascular imaging according to the local SAH pathway after senior discussion.
Administer fibrinolysis for presumed cerebral thrombosis.
Repeat CT in a month because the blood becomes more conspicuous with time.
Discharge because any negative CT excludes subarachnoid haemorrhage at all times.
Start oral migraine therapy and defer further evaluation for a week.
explanations: Correct: after >6 hours, a negative CT alone may be insufficient; further diagnostic testing is appropriate.
Fibrinolysis is dangerous if haemorrhage is present and no thrombotic diagnosis is established.
Blood becomes less visible over time; waiting is unsafe.
CT sensitivity is time dependent and a delayed negative CT may not reliably exclude SAH.
Thunderclap onset with meningism is a high-risk red flag; further SAH assessment is required.
pearl: A thunderclap headache requires SAH exclusion even with normal neurological examination, especially when CT is delayed beyond six hours.
pivot: For CT within six hours with high-quality scan and expert reading, some guidelines allow exclusion without LP in selected patients.

steps: ABC, BP, neurological exam, analgesia and avoid anticoagulation until bleed excluded.
Senior ED/neurology discussion, LP timing/CSF xanthochromia or CTA pathway depending local SAH algorithm.
Urgent neurosurgical transfer, BP/complication management and aneurysm treatment.
management.safety: LP is contraindicated in selected raised-ICP or coagulopathy situations; choose further tests with specialist input.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: An 82-year-old with non-valvular AF, previous TIA, hypertension and diabetes is not anticoagulated because he fell twice last year without major injury. BP is controlled and renal function is stable. He has no active bleeding.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate discussion?
options: Discuss an oral anticoagulant with individualised bleeding/falls mitigation and correct dose selection.
Withhold all antithrombotic treatment until he is free of falls for 12 months.
Recommend aspirin alone because any fall risk contraindicates all oral anticoagulation.
Give full-dose anticoagulant without checking kidney function, weight, interactions or patient preference.
Start dual antiplatelet therapy rather than anticoagulation irrespective of bleeding risk.
explanations: Correct: previous TIA and multiple CHA2DS2-VASc factors confer high embolic risk; falls alone rarely prohibit anticoagulation.
Falls risk alone usually does not outweigh high thromboembolic risk; modifiable contributors should be addressed.
Aspirin is not an effective equivalent substitute for AF stroke prevention in high-risk patients.
Proper DOAC choice/dose and shared bleeding-risk counselling are essential.
Dual antiplatelets are generally less effective and still cause bleeding; not routine AF stroke prevention.
pearl: High stroke-risk AF usually benefits from anticoagulation; bleeding and falls risks prompt mitigation and shared decisions, not automatic denial.
pivot: If active major bleeding or severe contraindication exists, temporarily withhold and discuss specialist alternatives.

steps: Assess stroke score, bleeding factors, falls, renal function, medications and patient goals.
Offer appropriate DOAC when suitable; check label dose rules, renal function and interactions; warfarin for specific mechanical valves/mitral stenosis.
Review antihypertensives, gait, orthostasis, environmental hazards, alcohol and avoid NSAIDs.
Reassess adherence, bleeding signs and kidney function periodically.
management.safety: Never empirically underdose a DOAC merely because a patient is old or has had falls.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A 19-year-old reports ingesting many aspirin tablets. He has tinnitus, vomiting, temperature 38.5°C, RR 38/min, pH 7.48, PCO2 low and bicarbonate 16 mmol/L. Salicylate level is high and rising.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Give acetazolamide to increase urine pH by causing bicarbonate loss.
Administer charcoal as the only treatment and discharge if vomiting resolves.
Intubate immediately without adjusting minute ventilation because alkalosis is harmful.
Give urinary alkalinisation with IV sodium bicarbonate plus potassium management and urgent toxicology/dialysis assessment.
Give empiric naloxone to reverse salicylate respiratory stimulation.
explanations: Acetazolamide may worsen systemic acidosis and is not a preferred method of alkalinisation.
Absorption/elimination and acid-base complications require inpatient treatment.
Unnecessary intubation can abruptly reduce respiratory compensation and worsen salicylate distribution to brain.
Correct: alkalinisation enhances renal elimination and reduces CNS penetration; severe features may mandate dialysis.
Naloxone is not a salicylate antidote.
pearl: Salicylate toxicity often causes mixed respiratory alkalosis and anion-gap metabolic acidosis; pH strongly affects CNS toxicity.
pivot: A small single ingestion in an asymptomatic patient can follow serial levels/observation without invasive treatment.

steps: ABC, serial blood gases, electrolytes, glucose, salicylate levels and renal function.
IV bicarbonate with potassium correction and frequent urine pH and serum pH monitoring.
Early nephrology/toxicology discussion for severe neurologic changes, refractory acidosis or high/rising concentrations.
Avoid intubation unless necessary; maintain required minute ventilation if performed.
management.safety: Hypokalaemia makes urinary alkalinisation difficult; monitor and replace potassium carefully.
management.local: Study guidance only. Follow current emergency department pathways, senior advice, patient factors and verified prescribing references.

stem: A 33-year-old asks to restart combined oral contraception. She has episodic migraine with visual zig-zag lights lasting 20 minutes before headache, smokes socially, BP 118/72 mmHg and no personal VTE history.
ask: Which method advice is MOST appropriate?
options: Recommend no contraception until migraine resolves permanently.
Combined estrogen–progestin pill is preferred because her BP is normal.
Use aspirin daily to neutralise estrogen stroke risk.
Use higher estrogen dose to suppress cortical spreading depression.
Avoid estrogen-containing combined methods and offer progestin-only or non-hormonal contraception.
explanations: Safer effective alternatives are available.
Migraine with aura is an important contraindication to estrogen-containing combined contraception regardless of BP.
Aspirin does not negate the thrombotic contraindication.
Higher estrogen exposure can increase thrombosis risk rather than protect.
Correct: migraine with aura increases ischaemic stroke risk, magnified by exogenous estrogen.
pearl: Migraine with aura is a key contraindication to estrogen-containing combined hormonal contraception.
pivot: Migraine without aura has different risk classification depending on age, smoking and other vascular risks.

steps: Clarify reversible focal neurological symptoms versus nonspecific light sensitivity.
Discuss estrogen-related ischaemic stroke risk and individual comorbidities.
Progestin-only pill, implant, LNG/Cu IUD or barrier options according to preference and eligibility.
Contraceptive efficacy, side effects and migraine review.
management.safety: A new focal neurological headache pattern warrants medical evaluation, not automatic migraine labeling.
management.local: Educational sequence. Use current local obstetric/anaesthetic/neonatal protocols, gestational thresholds and multidisciplinary advice.

stem: A 2-year-old has not developed meaningful words, does not consistently respond to her name and prefers lining up toys. She makes limited eye contact but hears television advertisements from another room. Parents are concerned about autism.
ask: Which evaluation is MOST appropriate?
options: Start methylphenidate to improve attention and speech.
Delay referral until age five because toddlers often speak late.
Reassure that repetitive play is universal and no assessment is indicated.
Diagnose autism immediately without hearing assessment because she can hear TV.
Refer for comprehensive developmental assessment including formal audiology, language and social-communication assessment.
explanations: Stimulants are not a treatment for autism-related communication delay.
Early identification and interventions are beneficial.
Combined social/communication concerns and repetitive behaviour warrant evaluation.
Response to sound does not exclude partial hearing loss; ASD assessment needs broad developmental evaluation.
Correct: speech delay and social differences need evaluation for ASD and hearing/language impairment.
pearl: Hearing loss, developmental language disorder and ASD can overlap; formal hearing testing is a key part of assessment.
pivot: If a child has normal social reciprocity and isolated articulation difficulty, language disorder may be more likely.

steps: Communication, social reciprocity, play, motor, adaptive skills, regression and family history.
Audiology even if child reacts to loud or preferred sounds.
Speech-language therapy and early intervention while multidisciplinary ASD assessment proceeds.
Explain uncertainty without stigma, monitor co-occurring conditions.
management.safety: Loss of previously acquired skills warrants more urgent developmental/neurological assessment.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

stem: A 34-year-old pedestrian struck by a car has pelvic pain, unstable pelvic ring on gentle initial assessment and BP 76/46 mmHg. FAST is negative and there is no obvious external bleeding.
ask: What should happen immediately?
options: Give therapeutic heparin to prevent pelvic DVT immediately.
Apply correctly positioned pelvic binder, activate haemorrhage resuscitation and urgent pelvic trauma/IR support.
Transport to CT alone before giving any blood product.
Remove binder after one minute to reassess pelvis.
Repeat vigorous pelvic compression several times to confirm instability.
explanations: Anticoagulation increases active bleeding and is not first priority.
Correct: pelvic venous/bony bleeding can cause shock despite a negative FAST.
Unstable shock needs stabilisation and haemorrhage planning before unsafe transport.
Pelvic stabilisation should remain until specialist definitive management.
Repeated manipulation can dislodge clots and worsen haemorrhage.
pearl: An unstable pelvis with shock and negative FAST suggests retroperitoneal haemorrhage; binder placement at greater trochanters matters.
pivot: If a pelvic fracture is stable without bleeding physiology, analgesia and orthopaedic imaging/rehabilitation become priorities.

steps: Binder at greater trochanters, avoid repeat pelvic springing.
Activate trauma massive transfusion, haemostatic blood products and thermal/coagulation monitoring.
Consult pelvic surgeon/IR for packing, embolisation or fixation according to injury and resources.
Look for urethral injury, associated long-bone and abdominal trauma.
management.safety: Avoid urethral catheter until urethral injury is excluded when blood at meatus or pelvic red flags exist.
management.local: Study summary only: obtain appropriate consultant and multidisciplinary guidance, verified drugs and local operative protocols.

stem: A 46-year-old with known myasthenia gravis treated with pyridostigmine presents with rapidly worsening ptosis, dysphagia and breathlessness after pneumonia. Single breath count is 8, forced vital capacity low, and she has no diarrhoea, sweating or muscle fasciculations.
ask: Which management is MOST appropriate?
options: Admit to critical care for respiratory monitoring/support and initiate rapid immunomodulation for myasthenic crisis.
Give repeated oral pyridostigmine doses without monitoring breathing.
Treat as anxiety and discharge because oxygen saturation is still 97%.
Give IV magnesium to improve neuromuscular transmission.
Give high-dose benzodiazepine to control dyspnoea.
explanations: Correct: infection-triggered ventilatory/bulbar failure requires airway planning plus IVIG/plasma exchange under neurology.
Bulbar and respiratory weakness risks airway failure; extra oral drugs do not provide adequate rescue.
SpO2 may stay normal until late in neuromuscular ventilatory failure.
Magnesium can worsen myasthenic weakness.
Sedation worsens respiratory compromise.
pearl: In neuromuscular failure, respiratory muscle weakness and bulbar signs matter more than resting oxygen saturation.
pivot: Cholinergic crisis may include weakness plus muscarinic excess such as diarrhoea, salivation and fasciculations.

steps: Urgent ICU/anaesthesia/neurology assessment, serial VC/NIF and aspiration risk assessment.
Antibiotics for pneumonia chosen to avoid myasthenia-worsening agents.
IVIG or plasma exchange, immunotherapy adjustment and ventilatory support when required.
Bulbar strength, aspiration, secretion control and medication interactions.
management.safety: Avoid drugs known to worsen MG, including certain antibiotics and magnesium.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

context: Advanced GP psychiatry ethics and safe prescribing
stem: An 82-year-old who lives alone has fallen twice in six months. She takes nocturnal temazepam for six years, reports morning unsteadiness and wishes to reduce tablets. Cognition is intact and there is no alcohol misuse.
ask: Which plan is MOST appropriate?
options: Use a shared gradual taper with CBT for insomnia, falls assessment and regular review.
Increase temazepam to maintain uninterrupted sleep despite repeated falls.
Replace with long-term antipsychotic for insomnia without psychiatric illness.
Stop temazepam abruptly today because falls risk eliminates withdrawal risk.
Add an opioid analgesic to help overnight sleep.
explanations: Correct: address drug harm while avoiding withdrawal and supporting sleep with non-drug therapy.
Sedatives increase falls and cognitive impairment risks.
Antipsychotics have substantial adverse effects and are not routine insomnia treatments.
Abrupt cessation after years can cause rebound insomnia, autonomic withdrawal and seizures.
Opioid plus benzodiazepine increases respiratory depression and fall risk.
pearl: Deprescribing long-term hypnotics requires collaborative taper and non-drug sleep treatment; abrupt cessation is unsafe.
pivot: Short-term hypnotic use in selected acute scenarios may follow a limited-duration plan with reassessment.

steps: Falls, orthostasis, vision, other sedatives, sleep habits and dependence.
Shared stepwise temazepam reduction over weeks/months depending withdrawal response.
CBT-I and sleep timing strategies; physical balance and home-safety interventions.
Review withdrawal symptoms, sleep and falls, adjusting pace safely.
management.safety: Avoid rapid tapers in patients with prior withdrawal seizures or complex dependence.
management.local: Educational teaching, not individual clinical orders. Apply current local mental health law, safeguarding procedures and medication monitoring requirements.

stem: A 59-year-old hypertensive man develops abrupt maximal tearing chest pain radiating between the shoulder blades. Right-arm BP 190/100 mmHg, left-arm BP 155/90 mmHg. ECG has non-specific ST changes; he is stable and has a new diastolic murmur.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate immediate plan?
options: Perform exercise stress testing to discriminate angina from dissection.
Arrange urgent CT aortography with IV impulse control and immediate cardiothoracic/vascular surgical discussion.
Commence aspirin and therapeutic heparin before any further assessment.
Give oral calcium-channel blockade only, discharge if pain lessens.
Give fibrinolysis for presumed ACS and then obtain CT after chest pain resolves.
explanations: Stress testing is contraindicated in suspected acute dissection.
Correct: sudden tearing pain, BP differential and aortic regurgitation are classic red flags needing urgent CTA and HR/BP control.
Antithrombotics may be dangerous when dissection is a strong possibility.
An aortic emergency requires IV impulse control, immediate definitive imaging and surgical input.
Thrombolysis in aortic dissection may cause catastrophic bleeding and rupture.
pearl: Suspected acute aortic dissection is a reason to pause the usual ACS antithrombotic reflex until clarified.
pivot: If unstable with strong dissection signs, bedside echo/TEE and immediate surgical pathways may supersede transport for CT.

steps: ECG, bilateral arm pressures, IV access, analgesia, close monitoring and emergency surgical/cardiology call.
Titrated IV beta blocker first when appropriate to control HR; then additional BP lowering under specialist direction.
Urgent CTA chest/abdomen/pelvis if stable; look for Stanford type A versus B and malperfusion.
Type A needs immediate cardiac surgical assessment; uncomplicated type B often medical BP management with vascular surveillance.
management.safety: Avoid vasodilator monotherapy before controlling tachycardia as reflex tachycardia may worsen shear stress.
management.local: Exam teaching framework. Confirm drug doses, contraindications and treatment thresholds with current local protocols and supervising teams.

stem: A 9-month-old has episodic severe crying with knee flexion and pallor, then becomes quiet between episodes. Vomiting is non-bilious initially, and a small blood-streaked stool occurs. He is stable and has no peritonism. Ultrasound demonstrates ileocolic intussusception.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate next step?
options: Perform emergency laparotomy in all ultrasound-confirmed intussusceptions regardless of clinical status.
Start systemic steroids to reduce bowel-wall inflammation and observe.
Discharge because the child is calm between painful episodes.
Arrange urgent paediatric surgery/radiology assessment for pneumatic/hydrostatic enema reduction after stabilisation.
Give an oral laxative to soften stool before repeating ultrasound.
explanations: Surgery is for failed enema, perforation, peritonitis, unstable patient or lead point concerns.
Steroids do not mechanically reduce intussusception.
Symptom-free intervals are classic for intussusception and do not remove risk.
Correct: stable uncomplicated ileocolic intussusception is often reduced radiologically with surgical backup.
Mechanical bowel telescoping is not treated by laxatives and can progress to ischaemia.
pearl: Intermittent severe colicky pain with pallor/lethargy in an infant is intussusception until proven otherwise, even without 'currant jelly stool'.
pivot: If unstable with peritonitis or perforation, immediate surgical exploration replaces enema reduction.

steps: NPO, IV access, fluid resuscitation if dehydrated/shocked, analgesia and monitor vomiting/abdominal signs.
Prompt paediatric surgical/radiology coordination for air or contrast enema in stable uncomplicated ileocolic disease.
Monitor after successful reduction for recurrence, feeding and pain; surgery if failed reduction or complications.
management.safety: Do not delay senior consultation when bilious emesis, guarding or shock is present.
management.local: Clinical teaching only. Use the relevant maternity/neonatal/paediatric escalation pathway and current local drug/weight-based protocols.

stem: An 82-year-old woman falls and has a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture. She is stable, anticoagulated for AF with apixaban, and in severe pain. She was independently mobile beforehand.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate initial ward management?
options: Give analgesia including a regional nerve block if feasible, assess anticoagulation and promptly coordinate operative fixation/arthroplasty.
Give thrombolysis before surgery to reverse venous clot risk.
Cancel all surgical planning for at least two weeks because she takes apixaban.
Keep her immobile without analgesia until surgery to avoid masking pain.
Discharge with a walking frame and oral opioids because she was independent before the fall.
explanations: Correct: elderly hip fracture care prioritises pain control, delirium prevention, optimisation and timely surgery.
Fibrinolysis is unrelated and hazardous in an acute fracture.
Surgery timing depends on last dose, renal function and neuraxial/anesthetic strategy, not an automatic fortnight delay.
Untreated pain increases delirium and physiological stress; analgesia should not wait.
A displaced femoral neck fracture requires inpatient surgical and multidisciplinary management.
pearl: Timely hip-fracture care includes analgesia, functional baseline, delirium prevention and shared perioperative anticoagulant planning.
pivot: A stable minimally displaced fracture in a highly selected patient may have a different fixation plan, but mobilisation and specialist review still matter.

steps: Analgesia with fascia iliaca block where indicated, pressure area care, glucose/renal review and delirium risk assessment.
Orthopaedic/anaesthetic coordination for timely fixation versus arthroplasty and timing after apixaban review.
Manage fluid/electrolytes, anaemia and falls risk without unnecessary delays.
Early mobilisation, VTE prophylaxis when appropriate, osteoporosis treatment and rehabilitation.
management.safety: Balance anticoagulant reversal/timing against surgical delay and bleeding; consult neuraxial anaesthesia requirements.
management.local: Apply current hospital antibiotics, imaging, procedural and anticoagulation guidance with surgical and critical-care supervision.

context: Advanced psychiatry primary care and medication safety
stem: A 66-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis presents with mouth ulcers, diarrhoea and fever. A medication review reveals that a new prescription was transcribed as methotrexate 15 mg DAILY instead of the intended 15 mg ONCE WEEKLY; she took it for five consecutive days. Neutrophils 0.6 × 10^9/L and platelets 54 × 10^9/L.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate immediate response?
options: Stop methotrexate, urgently admit/contact toxicology–haematology and initiate folinic acid rescue with infection and organ-function monitoring.
Give a live vaccine immediately to prevent infection while neutropenic.
Give folic acid alone at usual weekly supplement dose and arrange repeat blood count in a month.
Continue methotrexate at the correct weekly interval because toxicity will resolve with time.
Prescribe trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole because it reduces methotrexate-related marrow suppression.
explanations: Correct: potentially fatal medication error with mucositis and pancytopenia needs urgent rescue and supportive management.
Live vaccines are unsafe in profound immunosuppression and do not treat neutropenic sepsis.
Ordinary folic acid supplementation is not adequate rescue for major methotrexate toxicity.
Serious methotrexate toxicity is already present; further doses are dangerous.
Trimethoprim can potentiate methotrexate toxicity and marrow suppression; avoid harmful interactions.
pearl: Low-dose methotrexate for inflammatory disease is usually WEEKLY, not daily; dosing errors can cause severe mucositis and marrow failure.
pivot: High-dose methotrexate used in oncology has different planned schedules and formal leucovorin rescue/level monitoring protocols.

steps: Withhold methotrexate, hospitalise, contact poison centre/toxicology and haematology immediately.
Folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue according to toxicity protocol; consider supportive measures based on renal function and severity.
Check FBC, renal/liver function, electrolytes, cultures; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics promptly for febrile neutropenia and transfusion support as indicated.
Document/report medication incident, reconcile medicine list, counsel once-weekly dosing and use safer prescriptions/packaging.
management.safety: Do not confuse folic acid prophylaxis with folinic acid rescue; review nephrotoxic and interacting drugs.
management.local: Educational safety guide: confirm treatment and statutory reporting with your local specialist guidelines and safeguarding law.

stem: A 19-year-old collapses after a long race on a humid day. Rectal temperature is 41.1°C and he is confused and combative. BP 102/60 mmHg, HR 146/min, skin hot and sweaty. There is no seizure.
ask: Which is the BEST immediate action?
options: Give paracetamol and wait for temperature to fall.
Give IV antibiotics as definitive heat-stroke therapy.
Advise him to drink water and walk home after resting.
Wait for CK, sodium and renal function results before cooling.
Begin rapid active whole-body cooling immediately with ABC support and critical-care assessment.
explanations: Antipyretics do not correct heat stroke caused by failed thermoregulation.
Infection may be evaluated but antibiotics do not replace cooling.
Confusion and dangerous hyperthermia mandate emergency treatment.
Laboratory tests should run concurrently; delaying cooling increases organ injury.
Correct: core temperature above 40°C plus CNS dysfunction is heat stroke; rapid cooling predicts outcome.
pearl: Sweating does not exclude heat stroke; hyperthermia plus CNS dysfunction is the defining emergency.
pivot: Heat exhaustion may cause dizziness and fatigue without significant CNS dysfunction and responds to cooling/hydration.

steps: Remove excess clothing, cold-water immersion when feasible or evaporative cooling with ice, monitor rectal temperature.
Airway, circulation, glucose and cautious isotonic fluids, prevent shivering.
CK, renal/liver tests, electrolytes, DIC, neurological status and urine output.
Avoid overcooling once approaching appropriate target; critical care for organ failure.
management.safety: Do not use antipyretics as substitute for physical cooling.
management.local: Study guidance only. Follow current emergency department pathways, senior advice, patient factors and verified prescribing references.

stem: A 32-year-old with two years of infertility has severe cyclical dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and an ultrasound showing a 4 cm ovarian endometrioma. She and her partner wish to conceive soon. Ovarian reserve testing is borderline.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate plan?
options: Suggest hysterectomy because endometriosis is a progressive disease.
Give antibiotics for presumed chronic ovarian infection without further assessment.
Arrange individualised fertility and endometriosis consultation, weighing assisted reproduction, pain and surgery risks.
Recommend combined oral contraceptive for two years as definitive fertility treatment.
Perform cystectomy automatically because removing any endometrioma improves ovarian reserve.
explanations: Hysterectomy ends fertility and is inappropriate when conception is desired.
Endometrioma is not ordinarily bacterial infection.
Correct: infertility and limited reserve require careful counselling before ovarian surgery.
Hormonal suppression treats pain but prevents conception while used.
Endometrioma surgery can damage ovarian reserve; decision depends on pain, malignancy suspicion and fertility strategy.
pearl: Surgery for endometrioma may relieve pain but reduce healthy ovarian tissue; fertility goals change choices.
pivot: In a patient not trying to conceive, hormonal suppression and analgesic strategies may be reasonable for symptom control.

steps: Partner semen, tubal function, ovulation, age/AMH and extent of endometriosis.
Fertility specialist review; discuss assisted reproduction and pros/cons of cystectomy.
Appropriate analgesia and nonhormonal supports while attempting conception.
Individualised plan with reproductive specialists and gynaecology.
management.safety: Do not remove endometrioma without discussing ovarian-reserve impact.
management.local: Educational sequence. Use current local obstetric/anaesthetic/neonatal protocols, gestational thresholds and multidisciplinary advice.

stem: A 4-year-old has periorbital swelling and ascites after a respiratory infection. Urine protein 4+, serum albumin 18 g/L, creatinine normal, BP 98/60 mmHg and no haematuria. He is alert with good perfusion.
ask: Which initial treatment is MOST appropriate?
options: Administer an aggressive IV fluid bolus to all oedematous children.
Perform routine kidney biopsy before any treatment in every typical preschool presentation.
Treat with anticoagulation for all nephrotic children irrespective of risk.
Give antibiotics alone for presumed post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Begin a paediatric nephrotic syndrome corticosteroid regimen after appropriate evaluation and carefully assess fluid status.
explanations: Oedema does not necessarily mean intravascular depletion; excess fluid risks pulmonary overload.
Biopsy is not always required initially in typical steroid-sensitive-age presentation.
Nephrosis increases thrombosis risk but anticoagulation is individualised.
Massive proteinuria and hypoalbuminaemia without haematuria/hypertension suggest nephrotic syndrome.
Correct: typical childhood nephrotic syndrome is often steroid-responsive minimal-change disease.
pearl: Nephrotic syndrome = heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema; always assess effective circulation, infection and thrombosis risks.
pivot: If hypertension, gross haematuria, low complement or kidney impairment occur, investigate atypical nephritic or secondary causes.

steps: BP, urine protein quantification, serum albumin, renal function, infection and intravascular state.
Paediatric nephrology-guided prednisolone protocol; salt balance and diuretics only after careful assessment.
Urine protein, weight, infection, thrombosis, renal function and steroid effects.
Relapse detection and when to seek urgent care for fever, pain, low urine.
management.safety: Severe intravascular depletion can coexist with oedema; check perfusion before diuresis.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

context: Advanced surgical and acute speciality decisions
stem: A 25-year-old with UC reports 10 bloody stools daily, temperature 38.6°C, HR 118/min, Hb 93 g/L and CRP 98 mg/L. Abdominal film shows a transverse colon of 5.4 cm without free air. Stool infection samples are pending.
ask: Which initial inpatient management is MOST appropriate?
options: Admit for IV corticosteroids, VTE prophylaxis and close surgical/gastroenterology monitoring while excluding infection.
Use oral mesalazine alone without observations or electrolyte checks.
Give high-dose loperamide to stop bloody diarrhoea and discharge.
Delay all treatment until stool cultures return negative.
Perform immediate total colectomy in every case without steroid trial.
explanations: Correct: acute severe UC requires intensive medical therapy, infection testing and early rescue/surgery planning.
Oral therapy alone is inadequate in severe systemic colitis.
Antimotility agents may worsen severe colitis/toxic megacolon.
Exclude infection rapidly, but urgent severe-colitis therapy should not await prolonged results.
Surgery is essential for complications/refractory disease but not all severe presentations.
pearl: Acute severe UC is defined by frequent bloody stools plus systemic toxicity; plan rescue therapy by day-3 response.
pivot: Perforation, uncontrolled bleeding or toxic megacolon with deterioration necessitates urgent surgery.

steps: Stool frequency, vital signs, FBC/CRP, electrolytes and stool C. difficile testing.
IV corticosteroid and VTE prophylaxis unless contraindicated, fluid/electrolyte replacement and nutrition.
Daily stool count, CRP and abdominal signs; early gastro and colorectal surgery review.
Rescue infliximab/ciclosporin or colectomy if failure or complications.
management.safety: Avoid opioids, antidiarrhoeals and unnecessary barium enemas in severe colitis.
management.local: Study summary only: obtain appropriate consultant and multidisciplinary guidance, verified drugs and local operative protocols.

stem: A 42-year-old with episodic severe headache, palpitations and sweating has a 4 cm adrenal mass and plasma metanephrines four times the upper limit. He is booked for surgery in four weeks. BP between episodes is 150/90 mmHg.
ask: Which preoperative medication strategy is MOST appropriate?
options: Give loop diuretic to cause further volume contraction before operation.
Start alpha blockade first with salt/fluid optimisation; add beta blocker later only if indicated.
Avoid any blockade and operate urgently with usual anaesthesia.
Start a beta blocker immediately without alpha blockade to control tachycardia.
Give calcium supplements to block catecholamine release.
explanations: Patients are often volume contracted and need preoperative volume expansion.
Correct: alpha blockade precedes beta blockade before pheochromocytoma surgery.
Catecholamine release during surgery can provoke life-threatening crises.
Unopposed alpha-adrenergic activity can precipitate hypertensive crisis.
Calcium is not a specific blockade of catecholamine physiology.
pearl: Phaeochromocytoma surgery requires alpha-adrenergic blockade before beta blockade and careful volume preparation.
pivot: A nonsecretory adrenal incidentaloma with negative endocrine testing follows different evaluation and surgical indications.

steps: Metanephrine evaluation and imaging guided by endocrine service.
Alpha antagonist titration with BP monitoring, encourage appropriate salt/fluid restoration.
Add beta blocker only after adequate alpha blockade; discuss anaesthetic plan.
Experienced adrenal surgical team, intraoperative haemodynamic readiness and long-term surveillance.
management.safety: Never give isolated beta blockade before alpha blockade in confirmed catecholamine-secreting tumour.
management.local: Clinical educational outline only: review patient-specific contraindications and current treatment guidelines before prescribing.

skill: Acceptance and commitment therapy for chronic pain
context: Advanced GP psychiatry ethics and safe prescribing
stem: A 45-year-old with chronic low back pain has no red flags on examination and has completed appropriate investigations. He avoids movement for fear of pain, has stopped hobbies and feels frustrated with repeated unsuccessful attempts to eliminate every sensation. He asks about psychological treatment.
ask: Which explanation of ACT is MOST accurate?
options: ACT instructs the patient to ignore serious neurological red flags even if new weakness develops.
ACT uses exposure only after all distressing thoughts have been permanently suppressed.
ACT teaches acceptance of pain while clarifying values, defusing unhelpful thoughts and gradually re-engaging in meaningful activity.
ACT aims to remove every painful sensation before the patient resumes valued activity.
ACT is a medication regimen combining an antidepressant and anticonvulsant.
explanations: Acceptance never replaces assessment of new medical danger signs.
ACT teaches willingness and flexible action in the presence of difficult thoughts and sensations.
Correct: ACT targets relationship to pain and functional participation rather than direct pain suppression.
ACT focuses on psychological flexibility and values-led behaviour despite discomfort, not guaranteed symptom eradication.
ACT is a psychological behavioural therapy, not a pharmacological combination.
pearl: ACT's hexaflex develops acceptance, cognitive defusion, present-moment contact, self-as-context, values and committed action.
pivot: If acute cauda equina or other neurological red flags appear, urgent medical evaluation supersedes a chronic-pain behavioural plan.

steps: Medical red flags, function, sleep, mood, avoidance and patient-defined goals.
Values clarification, defusion and acceptance skills; small graded actions toward meaningful goals.
Combine with appropriate physiotherapy, pacing and medical pain management.
Measure function, activity and quality of life as well as pain severity.
management.safety: ACT should not imply pain is imaginary or that all physical treatments are unnecessary.
management.local: Educational teaching, not individual clinical orders. Apply current local mental health law, safeguarding procedures and medication monitoring requirements.
